title: Speed of Light in Vacuum (c)
answer: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second (approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s or 186,282 miles per second). Denoted by the physical constant 'c'.
highlights: Exact Value (SI): 299,792,458 m/s
Metric Approximation: 300,000 km/s (3 × 10⁸ m/s)
Imperial Approximation: ~186,282 miles/second
Significance: Universal physical constant and upper limit for speed of energy, matter, and information

title: Value of Pi (π)
answer: The value of Pi (π) is approximately 3.14159265359... (commonly represented as 22/7 or 3.14). It is defined as the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
highlights: Decimal Approximation: 3.141592653589793...
Fractional Approximation: 22/7 (Accurate to 2 decimal places)
Mathematical Nature: Irrational and transcendental number

title: Planck Constant (h)
answer: The Planck constant (h) is exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ Joule-seconds (J·s). It is the fundamental physical constant relating the energy of a photon to its frequency (E = hν).
highlights: Exact SI Value: h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s (or kg·m²·s⁻¹)
Reduced Planck Constant (ħ): ħ = h / (2π) ≈ 1.054571817 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s
Photon Energy Formula: E = hν = hc / λ
Significance: Foundation of quantum mechanics and defines the kilogram in the SI system

title: Newtonian Constant of Gravitation (G)
answer: The Universal Gravitational Constant (G) is approximately 6.67430 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² (m³·kg⁻¹·s⁻²). It represents the proportionality constant in Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation.
highlights: Recommended Value (CODATA): G = 6.67430(15) × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²
Universal Law of Gravitation: F = G · (m₁ · m₂) / r²
First Measured By: Henry Cavendish in 1798 using a torsion balance

title: Avogadro Constant (N_A)
answer: The Avogadro constant (N_A) is defined as exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ reciprocal moles (mol⁻¹). It represents the number of constituent particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) in one mole of a substance.
highlights: Exact SI Value: N_A = 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
Definition: The number of particles per mole of substance
Named After: Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro
Relation to Gas: 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 litres at STP (0 °C, 1 atm)

title: Standard Acceleration Due to Gravity (g)
answer: The standard acceleration due to Earth's gravity at sea level is standardly defined as 9.80665 m/s² (commonly rounded to 9.8 m/s² or 32.174 ft/s²).
highlights: Standard Value: g = 9.80665 m/s² (≈ 9.8 m/s²)
Formula: g = G · M / R² (where M is Earth's mass, R is Earth's radius)
Variation: Stronger at the poles (~9.832 m/s²) and weaker at the equator (~9.780 m/s²) due to Earth's oblateness

title: Boltzmann Constant (k or k_B)
answer: The Boltzmann constant (k_B) is exactly 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ Joules per Kelvin (J/K). It relates the average relative thermal kinetic energy of particles in a gas with the thermodynamic temperature.
highlights: Exact SI Value: k_B = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J·K⁻¹
Ideal Gas Law Relation: R = N_A · k_B
Entropy Equation: S = k_B · ln(Ω) (engraved on Ludwig Boltzmann's tombstone)

title: Elementary Charge (e)
answer: The elementary charge (e) is exactly 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ Coulombs (C). An electron has a charge of -e, and a proton has a charge of +e.
highlights: Exact SI Value: e = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
Electron Charge: -1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
Proton Charge: +1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
First Measured By: Robert A. Millikan in the oil drop experiment (1909)

title: Newton's Three Laws of Motion
answer: Newton's Laws of Motion state: 1st Law (Inertia): An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force. 2nd Law: Force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma). 3rd Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
highlights: 1st Law (Law of Inertia): Objects resist changes in their state of motion
2nd Law (Force Law): F = dp/dt = m · a (Force = mass × acceleration)
3rd Law (Action-Reaction): F_AB = -F_BA (Forces always occur in matched action-reaction pairs)
Published: In Principia Mathematica (1687)

title: Ohm's Law (V = I · R)
answer: Ohm's law states that the electrical current (I) flowing through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage (V) across the two points and inversely proportional to the resistance (R): V = I · R.
highlights: Formula: V = I · R (Voltage = Current × Resistance)
Current: I = V / R (measured in Amperes, A)
Resistance: R = V / I (measured in Ohms, Ω)
Power Equations: P = V · I = I² · R = V² / R (measured in Watts, W)

title: Four Laws of Thermodynamics
answer: The Four Laws of Thermodynamics govern energy and heat transfer: Zeroth Law (Thermal equilibrium / temperature definition), First Law (Energy conservation: ΔU = Q - W), Second Law (Entropy of an isolated system always increases: ΔS ≥ 0), and Third Law (Entropy approaches a constant zero as temperature reaches absolute zero: T → 0 K).
highlights: Zeroth Law: If systems A and B are in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other
First Law: Conservation of Energy (ΔU = Q - W)
Second Law: Total entropy of an isolated system never decreases (Heat flows spontaneously only from hotter to colder)
Third Law: Absolute zero (0 Kelvin / -273.15 °C) cannot be reached in a finite number of steps

title: Einstein's Mass-Energy Equivalence (E = mc²)
answer: Einstein's mass-energy equivalence equation E = mc² asserts that mass and energy are interchangeable. The energy (E) of a physical system is equal to its relativistic mass (m) multiplied by the square of the speed of light (c²).
highlights: Formula: E = mc² (where E = Energy in Joules, m = Mass in kg, c = Speed of light ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
Factor: c² ≈ 9 × 10¹⁶ m²/s² (explaining why tiny amounts of mass release immense energy in nuclear reactions)
Published: By Albert Einstein in his 1905 Annus Mirabilis paper

title: Photosynthesis — Biological Process & Chemical Equation
answer: Photosynthesis is the biological process by which green plants, algae, and cyanobacteria convert sunlight, water (H2O), and carbon dioxide (CO2) into glucose (C6H12O6) and oxygen (O2).
highlights: Balanced Chemical Equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + Light Energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Organelle: Chloroplasts containing the green pigment Chlorophyll
Two Stages: Light-dependent reactions (Thylakoid membrane) and Calvin Cycle (Stroma)

title: Cellular Respiration — Chemical Equation & ATP Generation
answer: Cellular respiration is the metabolic process that breaks down glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy stored in ATP molecules: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ~36–38 ATP.
highlights: Chemical Equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + Energy (~36–38 ATP)
Three Main Stages: 1) Glycolysis (Cytoplasm), 2) Krebs / Citric Acid Cycle (Mitochondrial Matrix), 3) Electron Transport Chain (Inner Mitochondrial Membrane)
Powerhouse of the Cell: Mitochondria

title: Water (H₂O) — Chemical Formula & Properties
answer: The chemical formula of water is H₂O (two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom). Its systematic IUPAC name is Oxidane or Dihydrogen Monoxide.
highlights: Chemical Formula: H₂O
Molar Mass: 18.01528 g/mol
Freezing Point: 0 °C (32 °F / 273.15 K)
Boiling Point: 100 °C (212 °F / 373.15 K) at 1 atm
Density: Maximum density of 1.000 g/cm³ at 3.98 °C (anomalous expansion of water)

title: Common Salt (NaCl / Sodium Chloride) — Chemical Formula
answer: The chemical formula of common table salt is NaCl (Sodium Chloride). It is an ionic compound composed of a 1:1 ratio of sodium cations (Na⁺) and chloride anions (Cl⁻).
highlights: Chemical Formula: NaCl
Chemical Name: Sodium Chloride
Molar Mass: 58.44 g/mol
Crystal Structure: Face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice
Melting Point: 801 °C (1,474 °F)

title: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) — Chemical Formula & Structure
answer: The chemical formula of glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆. It is a simple monosaccharide sugar and the primary energy source for cellular metabolism in living organisms.
highlights: Chemical Formula: C₆H₁₂O₆
Molar Mass: 180.156 g/mol
Type: Aldohexose (6-carbon monosaccharide with an aldehyde group)
Role in Body: Circulates in blood as blood sugar; stored as glycogen in liver and muscles

title: Baking Soda (NaHCO₃ / Sodium Bicarbonate)
answer: The chemical formula of baking soda is NaHCO₃ (Sodium Bicarbonate or Sodium Hydrogen Carbonate). It is a white crystalline chemical compound widely used as a leavening agent.
highlights: Chemical Formula: NaHCO₃
Chemical Name: Sodium Hydrogen Carbonate / Sodium Bicarbonate
Molar Mass: 84.007 g/mol
Reaction with Acid: NaHCO₃ + H⁺ → Na⁺ + H₂O + CO₂↑ (releases carbon dioxide gas which causes dough to rise)

title: Washing Soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O / Sodium Carbonate Decahydrate)
answer: The chemical formula of washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (Sodium Carbonate Decahydrate). Anhydrous sodium carbonate is commonly known as soda ash (Na₂CO₃).
highlights: Chemical Formula: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O
Chemical Name: Sodium Carbonate Decahydrate
Industrial Process: Manufactured via the Solvay Process
Use: Water softening, detergent booster, glass and paper manufacturing

title: Sulfuric Acid (H₂SO₄) — The King of Chemicals
answer: The chemical formula of sulfuric acid is H₂SO₄. It is a strong mineral acid with strong hygroscopic and oxidizing properties, widely referred to as the 'King of Chemicals' due to its vast industrial applications.
highlights: Chemical Formula: H₂SO₄
Molar Mass: 98.079 g/mol
Historical Name: Oil of Vitriol
Industrial Production: Contact Process
Applications: Lead-acid battery electrolyte, fertilizer (superphosphate) manufacturing

title: Hydrochloric Acid (HCl / Muriatic Acid)
answer: The chemical formula of hydrochloric acid is HCl (an aqueous solution of hydrogen chloride). It is a strong acid naturally found in gastric juice (stomach acid) with a pH of 1.5 to 3.5.
highlights: Chemical Formula: HCl (aq)
Molar Mass: 36.46 g/mol
Traditional Name: Muriatic Acid / Spirits of Salt
Biological Role: Produced by parietal cells in gastric glands to aid digestion and kill bacteria

title: Nitric Acid (HNO₃ / Aqua Fortis)
answer: The chemical formula of nitric acid is HNO₃. It is a highly corrosive, toxic mineral acid, historically called aqua fortis (strong water), used extensively in manufacturing explosives (TNT, nitroglycerin) and fertilizers.
highlights: Chemical Formula: HNO₃
Molar Mass: 63.01 g/mol
Industrial Synthesis: Ostwald Process (oxidation of ammonia)
Aqua Regia Mixture: 1 part concentrated HNO₃ to 3 parts concentrated HCl dissolves gold and platinum

title: Methane (CH₄) — Structure & Natural Gas Component
answer: The chemical formula of methane is CH₄ (one carbon atom bonded covalently to four hydrogen atoms in a tetrahedral geometry). It is the simplest alkane and the main constituent of natural gas and biogas.
highlights: Chemical Formula: CH₄
Molecular Geometry: Tetrahedral (bond angle 109.5°)
Molar Mass: 16.04 g/mol
Greenhouse Gas: Potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential ~28–36 times that of CO₂ over a 100-year timescale

title: Bleaching Powder (CaOCl₂ / Calcium Hypochlorite)
answer: The chemical formula of bleaching powder is CaOCl₂ (Calcium Oxychloride or Calcium Hypochlorite, Ca(OCl)₂). It is widely used as a disinfectant and water purification agent.
highlights: Chemical Formula: CaOCl₂ [or Ca(OCl)₂]
Chemical Name: Calcium Hypochlorite / Calcium Oxychloride
Preparation: Action of chlorine gas on dry slaked lime: Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O
Uses: Disinfecting drinking water, bleaching cotton and linen in textile industry

keywords: chemical formula of plaster of paris
title: Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O) & Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O)
answer: The chemical formula of Plaster of Paris (POP) is CaSO₄·½H₂O (Calcium Sulfate Hemihydrate). It is produced by heating gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O / Calcium Sulfate Dihydrate) to 373 K (100 °C).
highlights: Plaster of Paris Formula: CaSO₄·½H₂O (or 2CaSO₄·H₂O)
Gypsum Formula: CaSO₄·2H₂O (Calcium Sulfate Dihydrate)
Setting Reaction: CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O (hardens into solid gypsum)
Uses: Bone fracture casts, sculpture making, decorative ceiling designs

title: DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid) — Structure & Base Pairing
answer: DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid) is the molecule carrying genetic instructions in all known living organisms. It consists of a double helix of two polynucleotide chains paired via hydrogen bonds: Adenine pairs with Thymine (A=T with 2 hydrogen bonds), and Guanine pairs with Cytosine (G≡C with 3 hydrogen bonds).
highlights: Full Form: Deoxyribonucleic Acid
Structure: Double Helix discovered by James Watson and Francis Crick (1953) with Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51
Nitrogenous Bases: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C)
Chargaff's Rule: Amount of Adenine equals Thymine (A=T), and Guanine equals Cytosine (G=C)
